source: Weber, Binder & Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies
finding: Natural frequency format helps, but most people still fail. Many people given frequencies convert them back to probabilities. The calculation format they actually use matters more than the format shown.
numbers: N=180 students (114 + 66 replication), 360 inferences, two tasks. Correct: 20% with probability format, 36% with frequency format. Heroin task 51% vs car accident task 22% with frequencies. 49% of people shown frequencies still calculated with probabilities; only 18% shown probabilities switched to frequencies. Correct by calculation format: frequencies used 61% (shown freq) and 53% (shown prob); probabilities used 13% and 9%.
limits: Mostly maths-education students, German, written problems, one lab. Task story changed accuracy a lot (51% vs 22%). Higher-ability subgroup (n=42) scored 50% vs 21%.
agent_relevance: The route the solver takes matters, not the way the data is displayed. Our code should convert any probability input to counts of cases itself, then add counts. Do not leave the conversion to the model.

source: Weber, Binder & Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies
finding: Cites the McDowell and Jacobs (2017) meta-analysis: natural frequencies lift correct Bayesian answers from 4% to 24%. So three quarters still fail with the best format.
numbers: Meta-analysis figure as quoted: 24% correct with natural frequencies vs 4% with probabilities.
limits: Second-hand figure. The original meta-analysis was not opened (download failed).
agent_relevance: The famous natural-frequency fix is a modest gain, not a cure. Do not count on formatting alone; compute the posterior in code.

source: Weber, Binder & Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies
finding: Individual differences dominate. Fixed effects (format) explain little variance; person-level differences explain most.
numbers: GLMM: marginal R2 = 0.065 (fixed effects), conditional R2 = 0.685 (with person intercepts). Calculation format b=9.85, SE 3.85, p=0.01; interaction b=4.85, p=0.03.
limits: Student sample. Within-person logistic model, so coefficients are large and unstable.
agent_relevance: Same prompt, different solver, very different results. For a model agent, the strategy chosen at the start (counts or probabilities) predicts success, so choose it by rule.

source: Weber, Binder & Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies
finding: Einstellung-style explanation: school trained people on probability formulas, so they switch to them even when counts are easier. Ability level did not change the switching rate.
numbers: Frequency algorithm used in 32% of solutions by the strong maths subgroup vs 35% in the rest (t(358)=-0.506, p=.613), though accuracy differed 50% vs 21%.
limits: Explanation is the authors' reading of written work, not an experiment that manipulates habit.
agent_relevance: A model has the same pull toward symbolic formulas (see Araya 2025). Force the count-based path in the scaffold.

source: Heit (2000) Properties of inductive reasoning
finding: Review of the category-based induction phenomena: similarity, typicality, specificity, sample size and premise diversity all strengthen inductions. The diversity effect is the least robust one.
numbers: Diversity: found in adults in several studies; not found in 9-year-olds with specific conclusions (Gutheil and Gelman; Lopez et al. 1992); Heit and Hahn (1999) found it in children with pictures of dolls and hats: 74% of critical test items chose the diverse set (ages 5 to 8).
limits: Review. Percentages are from the review text, not re-derived. Mixed child evidence.
agent_relevance: Do not treat diverse evidence as stronger by default. Check what the property is and what the reasoner knows.

source: Heit (2000) Properties of inductive reasoning
finding: Culture and knowledge change the diversity effect. Itzaj Maya adults did not show it for disease-spread arguments, but did for a corn-cob sampling problem. Korean students did show it.
numbers: Lopez et al. (1997) Itzaj: no diversity effect on arguments about living things, sometimes preferred homogeneous premises. Choi, Nisbett and Smith (1997): effect found in Korean students.
limits: Cited from the review; original papers not opened. Itzaj explained their choices with disease-transmission knowledge that conflicted with diversity.
agent_relevance: Diversity is a rule that depends on background knowledge. Rival knowledge can beat the rule, so an agent needs to look at why the property might spread.

source: Heit (2000) Properties of inductive reasoning
finding: Non-monotonicity: adding a premise can make an argument weaker. The argument 'flies and orangutans, so bees' was judged weaker than 'flies, so bees'. Explained by the premise set bringing up a broader category where the premises are less typical.
numbers: Pattern replicated with Korean undergraduates (Choi et al. 1997); some evidence in 5-year-olds and more consistent evidence in 9-year-olds (Lopez et al. 1992). Sloman (1993) feature exclusion effect is a related violation.
limits: Review; effect sizes not given in the review.
agent_relevance: Models trained on 'more evidence is stronger' will miss this (see Han et al. 2024). The scaffold should check the category the premises jointly suggest.

source: Heit (2000) Properties of inductive reasoning
finding: Heit's Bayesian model: the novel property is a cue to retrieve familiar properties. Prior beliefs over how widely the property is shared give typicality, similarity and diversity effects without special rules.
numbers: Worked table with four hypotheses for the Cows/Sheep example. Predicts independent influence of premise typicality; the review flags that it may struggle with nonmonotonicity and needs property-specific priors.
limits: Qualitative. Only a sketch with illustrative numbers, not a fitted model in this paper.
agent_relevance: A usable plan: write the prior over 'how many categories share this property' as an explicit table in code and update it.

source: Heit (2000) Properties of inductive reasoning
finding: Sample size effect is robust in adults. One observed obese Barratos member did not give a strong inference about all; 3 or 20 members gave stronger ones. Children aged 9 and under give mixed results.
numbers: Inferences stronger with 1, 3, then 20 observed members, and still short of 100% for small samples.
limits: Review; no counts.
agent_relevance: Generalisation strength should scale with sample count, which code can check. Do not let a model assert 'all' from one case.

source: Sides, Osherson, Bonini & Viale (2002) On the reality of the conjunction fallacy
finding: Conjunction fallacy is not just a word problem or a misread of 'probability'. It stayed about as common when people bet on a sentence instead of rating probability.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=45 per condition): probability condition 3.4 errors of 9 (SD 2.55); betting 3.2 (SD 2.33), 36 of 45 bettors erred at least once. Exp 2 (Houston, 29 prob, 28 bet): 5.93 vs 4.86 errors of 9, t(55)=1.86, p<.07; all 29 probability participants erred at least once.
limits: One lab group. US undergraduates. Items were singular future events, not Linda.
agent_relevance: Bet-style framing is not a fix. A code-level check that P(A and B) <= P(A) is needed.

source: Sides, Osherson, Bonini & Viale (2002) On the reality of the conjunction fallacy
finding: Larger sample at a second site. Fallacy stayed high under both instructions. Rice students erred less than Houston students but not to zero.
numbers: Exp 3: 92 probability, 60 betting. 90 of 92 erred at least once; 4.33 of 9 errors (SD 1.61) vs betting 4.85 (SD 1.75), t(150)=1.88, p<.06. Item fallacy rates correlated across conditions r=.96. University effect F=27.6, p<.001.
limits: Exp 3 details are as parsed from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Higher-ability groups erred less, but never to zero. The check belongs in code, not in the model's judgement.

source: Sides, Osherson, Bonini & Viale (2002) On the reality of the conjunction fallacy
finding: Experiment 4 hid the unchosen sentence from a third-party reader, ruling out a reading of 'X' as 'X and not Y'. Fallacy rate was practically the same in explicit and implicit conditions.
numbers: One item attracted 46 fallacies out of 83 participants; of 39 who erred on only one of two items, 32 erred on item 2 and 7 on item 1.
limits: Item difficulty differs a lot: in Exp 1 one item drew 51 of 90 fallacies, another 19.
agent_relevance: The fallacy depends on item content (how much the evidence supports the extra detail). Test item by item.

source: Han & Budescu (2022) Recalibrating probabilistic forecasts to improve their accuracy
finding: Recalibrating forecasts with a single power parameter on log odds cut Brier scores sharply. Gains were largest for near-term horizons.
numbers: ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters; about 10,000 forecast distributions per indicator. Mean relative Brier improvement 0.569 (inflation), 0.452 (GDP), 0.574 (unemployment); 0.621, 0.539, 0.623 at the 1-year horizon. Distant horizons gained less.
limits: Economic experts. Parameters were fitted using the outcomes, so real out-of-sample gain is smaller. Some cases need de-extremizing (parameter < 1).
agent_relevance: Calibration can be fixed in code, but the direction (extremize or not) must be fitted on held-out data. Fits schema G4: no blind extremizing.

source: Han & Budescu (2022) Recalibrating probabilistic forecasts to improve their accuracy
finding: Literature on aggregate forecasting: extremizing helped in a 2000-forecaster tournament, but sometimes de-extremizing was better. Experts need less extremization than non-experts and the median needs less than the mean.
numbers: Baron et al. (2014), Mellers et al. (2014), Turner et al. (2014): the best model transforms individual forecasts first, then aggregates log odds.
limits: Second-hand summary; tournament papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Aggregating model samples needs care. Same-model samples are correlated, so extremizing could hurt. Test before use.

source: Li & Rui (2024) Dual traits in probabilistic reasoning of large language models
finding: Six LLMs follow Bayes' rule on an uncharacteristic description and largely ignore the base rate when the description is stereotypical. Matches a two-mode (System 1 / System 2) account.
numbers: Jason test, base rates 75% vs 25%. Uncharacteristic: posterior odds ratio 9 (normative) for GPT-4o, GPT-4 and Llama-3-70B; 8.86 Claude-3-Opus; 6.36 Gemini-1.5-Pro; 3 Mistral-Large; humans 2.25. Representative descriptions: LLM ratios 1.0 to 2.6, humans about 2.0.
limits: Human column is pooled from older replications at different base rates (0.7/0.3). Small test set, one task family.
agent_relevance: A model uses the base rate right only when the evidence carries no stereotype. Our code should do the Bayes update with the base rate fixed from the prompt.

source: Li & Rui (2024) Dual traits in probabilistic reasoning of large language models
finding: When asked to recall base rates itself, the model was inconsistent. Prompting to apply Bayes' rule did not change the pattern until the last, step-by-step prompt.
numbers: GPT-4o gave priors of 2 to 4% for a field when asked directly, but used 10 to 30% when judging a posterior. Four increasingly forceful prompts: correlations between posterior and similarity did not change.
limits: Single model on this test, three fields, one vignette.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone does not repair this. Fetch priors in a separate step, store them, and pass the stored number.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber & Goodman (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: Hypothesis search: ask the model for many natural-language rules, turn each into code, run the code on the given examples. This beat direct prompting on ARC.
numbers: 100-task ARC subset, GPT-4: direct prompting 17%, programs from direct generation 23%, programs from LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%, from human-selected hypotheses 33%. Human-written (LARC) hypotheses about the same. Non-LLM Icecuber solver 43%.
limits: 100-task sample. Cost is high (up to $1.5 to test one hypothesis with 8 programs and 2 feedback rounds). 64 hypotheses needed for a reasonable hit rate.
agent_relevance: This is the model for S2: candidate rules, then a code-run test. Filter by summarising to a smaller set.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber & Goodman (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: Much of the bottleneck is picking the right hypothesis, not writing the program. GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 of 100 tasks. Of the 30 tasks solved with summaries, 28 already had a correct hypothesis before summarising.
numbers: Human selection led to correct programs in 33 of 49 tasks (67%). Chain of thought with an intermediate language hypothesis and no programs dropped to 19%.
limits: Human annotation judged hypothesis correctness; single model (gpt-4-0314) for the main run.
agent_relevance: Verification by execution is the gain, not the verbal reasoning. Keep rule search tied to code.

source: Wang, Zelikman, Poesia, Pu, Haber & Goodman (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: On easy-to-code tasks the abstract-hypothesis step adds nothing. On SyGuS string tasks direct program generation already reached 94.3%, same as with hypotheses.
numbers: SyGuS: 94.3% both ways (8 programs, 2 feedback rounds); CrossBeam DSL baseline 74.8%. Three of five failures were errors in the dataset's own examples. With Parsel, human hypotheses reached 47.5% vs 37.5% direct, but LLM hypotheses got worse.
limits: Task-dependent. Parsel result reversed for model-written hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Do not add hypothesis search everywhere. Use it only when direct attempts fail a check (matches G1).

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement
finding: Language models are good at proposing rules and poor at applying them. With an external interpreter that filters rules, accuracy rose. When the model itself applied its own rules it fell sharply.
numbers: GPT-4. Task accuracy, IO prompting vs best refinement setting in Table 1: ACRE 28.0 vs 47 to 48; MiniSCAN 0.0 vs 46.0; List Functions 39.6 vs 52.0 (T=1,N=1). Applying own rules with the LM: MiniSCAN task accuracy fell from over 80% to nearly 0.
limits: MiniARC raw accuracy was worse with refinement (5.9 to 12.8) than IO (33.1). MiniSCAN did better with N=1 than N=5, a sign of overfitting to the exemplars.
agent_relevance: Matches G3: fitting examples is not proof. The check must be run by code, and rule application should also be done by code.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement
finding: Rule-based answers are more robust out of distribution than direct prompting, but not fully. Noise in the examples hurts the LM more than humans.
numbers: OOD tests with longer lists or larger grids: IO prompting dropped sharply; rule prompting dropped less. Noise: 12.5%, 25%, 50% of 8 exemplars corrupted; performance fell with a single bad example and kept falling, and an instruction to expect noise helped only partly. Pseudoword outputs lowered MiniSCAN accuracy.
limits: Human comparison run on a subset only; GPT-4 for main runs.
agent_relevance: Noise is real. The agent must allow a rule to leave some examples unexplained and report how many.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors & Kemp (2024) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: GPT-4 matches humans on most classic category-based induction phenomena; GPT-3.5 does not. The clearest failure of GPT-4 is non-monotonicity, where it gives the opposite answer for specific arguments.
numbers: 792 argument pairs; 110 human participants after 10 exclusions. 11 phenomena across mammals, birds, vehicles. GPT-4 agreed with humans on Similarity, Specificity, Typicality, Monotonicity. GPT-3.5 gave bimodal, order-sensitive answers. Humans themselves did not robustly show Diversity, Asymmetry or Inclusion fallacy; GPT-4 showed Diversity for general arguments, humans did not.
limits: gpt-4-0314, chat API, one response per pair. Sign test on direction only, not size. Human diversity effect was weaker than the textbook.
agent_relevance: Model similarity-coverage reasoning is decent. The exception cases are where more premises weaken the claim.

source: Macmillan-Scott & Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models
finding: Seven LLMs show irrationality on classic tasks, but mostly not the human way. Most wrong answers are illogical rather than biased, and the same model answers the same item differently across runs.
numbers: Each task prompted 10 times. GPT-4 correct with correct reasoning in 69.2%; Claude 2 55.0%. Llama 2 7B incorrect in 77.5%. GPT-3.5 human-like biased answers only 21.7% (50.8% including human-like correct). GPT-4 human-like (correct or biased) 73.3%; Llama 2 13B 8.3%.
limits: Tasks include Linda, Monty Hall, Wason. Many tasks may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a human bias list covers LLM errors. Inconsistency is itself a failure; run the same item several times and compare.

source: Araya (2025) Do chains of thoughts of LLMs suffer from hallucinations, cognitive biases or phobias in Bayesian reasoning
finding: With chain of thought, LLMs do not choose the natural-frequency strategy on their own. When told to use it, they follow it only some of the time and often get the arithmetic wrong.
numbers: Prompt variants add 'consider the Natural frequencies strategy proposed by Gigerenzer'. Example transcripts show a model applying it superficially and ending with a wrong 50% posterior. Persistent bias to symbolic reasoning.
limits: Few problems, qualitative transcripts; no accuracy table extracted. Treat as suggestive.
agent_relevance: Mirrors Weber et al. Strong reason to take the count conversion and the division out of the model's hands.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1983) Extensional versus intuitive reasoning (Linda)
finding: Original conjunction fallacy demonstration with the Linda story. A majority ranked 'bank teller and feminist' above 'bank teller'.
numbers: Not opened. Described in Sides et al. (2002) as a majority ranking the conjunction as more probable.
limits: Not read; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Source of the fallacy; verify numbers before citing.

source: Hertwig & Gigerenzer (1999) The 'conjunction fallacy' revisited
finding: Rival account: 'probability' is polysemous, so apparent conjunction errors may partly come from a conversational reading. Frequency wording reduces the effect.
numbers: Not opened. Cited in Sides et al. (2002) for polysemy.
limits: Not read. Sides et al. is the main test of this rival account and mostly goes against it.
agent_relevance: Wording alone is not the fix; use code.

source: McDowell & Jacobs (2017) Meta-analysis of the effect of natural frequencies on Bayesian reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of natural-frequency studies. Source of the 24% vs 4% summary used by Weber et al.
numbers: Not opened. Figures taken from Weber et al. (2018): 24% correct with frequencies, 4% with probabilities.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Check the moderators in the original before relying on it.
